subtopic_detail: preventing viral reactivation before rituximab in a patient with resolved hepatitis B infection
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man newly diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma who is due to start rituximab based chemotherapy next week.

He was born in Vietnam and came to Australia at nineteen. He has never had jaundice and has never been told he has a liver problem. His pre treatment screening shows hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis B core antibody positive and hepatitis B surface antibody positive at a protective level, with hepatitis B viral load undetectable. His alanine aminotransferase is normal, his liver ultrasound is normal and his hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology are negative. The haematology team have asked whether anything is needed before the first cycle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, cervical lymphadenopathy consistent with his lymphoma
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, core antibody positive, surface antibody positive at a protective level, hepatitis B viral load undetectable, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 45), liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before starting his chemotherapy?

options.text: No specific action, since a negative surface antigen indicates cleared infection
options.rationale: A negative surface antigen with positive core antibody means the virus is controlled by the immune system rather than eradicated, because covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei indefinitely. Removing B cell mediated immune control is precisely what allows that reservoir to reactivate. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Give a hepatitis B vaccine booster course before the first cycle of treatment
options.rationale: Vaccination generates surface antibody, which he already has at a protective level, and it does nothing about the intranuclear viral reservoir that reactivation arises from. Response to vaccination is also poor once chemotherapy has begun. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Commence antiviral prophylaxis before the immunosuppression begins
options.rationale: Rituximab depletes B cells and carries one of the highest risks of hepatitis B reactivation of any agent, including reverse seroconversion in people whose surface antigen is negative and core antibody positive, and the resulting hepatitis can be fulminant and fatal. Entecavir or tenofovir started before the first cycle prevents this and is continued for at least twelve months after the last dose, because the risk persists while B cell recovery is incomplete. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Monitor liver enzymes monthly and start an antiviral if the enzymes rise
options.rationale: Monitoring with on demand treatment is an accepted strategy only for patients at low reactivation risk, and it fails with rituximab because the viral load rises before the transaminases and the hepatitis can progress to liver failure faster than a monthly test detects. Waiting for enzyme rise means waiting for hepatocyte destruction to have begun. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Replace rituximab with a regimen that avoids B cell depleting monoclonal therapy
options.rationale: Rituximab substantially improves survival in this lymphoma and omitting it would trade a curable cancer outcome for a risk that effective prophylaxis reduces to a very low level. The hepatitis risk is managed pharmacologically rather than by compromising the oncological regimen. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

explanation.summary: Hepatitis B is never fully eradicated after infection, because covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei and is held in check by immune surveillance rather than removed. A surface antigen negative, core antibody positive pattern therefore represents resolved rather than absent infection, and immunosuppression can allow reverse seroconversion with reappearance of surface antigen and a viral load. Rituximab and other B cell depleting agents carry among the highest reactivation risks, and the resulting hepatitis may be severe or fatal. All patients should be screened for surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody before immunosuppression, and those at high risk receive entecavir or tenofovir prophylaxis started before treatment and continued for at least twelve months afterwards. Monitoring alone is reserved for low risk regimens, because viral load rises before transaminases do.
key_points: Covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocytes for life, so infection is controlled rather than cleared.
Core antibody positivity with a negative surface antigen indicates resolved infection at risk of reactivation.
Rituximab and other B cell depleting agents carry the highest reactivation risk.
Prophylaxis starts before immunosuppression and continues at least twelve months after the last dose.
Screening before immunosuppression should include surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody.
explanation.pearls: Order hepatitis B core antibody rather than surface antigen alone before any B cell depleting therapy, because a patient who has cleared surface antigen still harbours intranuclear viral DNA and rituximab can drive reverse seroconversion into a fulminant hepatitis.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Hepatitis B

subtopic_detail: applying the diameter and growth thresholds for repair to an incidentally found aortic aneurysm in a fit older man
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 71 year old man after an abdominal ultrasound arranged for intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, which showed gallstones and an incidental infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.8 cm in maximum anteroposterior diameter.

He has no back pain and no abdominal pain related to the aneurysm, and his abdomen is not tender. He smoked twenty cigarettes a day for forty years and stopped two years ago. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and his blood pressure today is 138/82 mmHg. He walks his dog for an hour daily without limitation and lives independently. He has no family history of aneurysm. A scan performed eleven months ago for renal colic reported the aorta as 4.6 cm, which no one had mentioned to him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with a pulsatile mass palpable above the umbilicus, femoral and pedal pulses present and equal, no abdominal bruit, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Current ultrasound 4.8 cm infrarenal aneurysm, ultrasound eleven months ago reported 4.6 cm, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.5), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for urgent vascular surgical repair within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Urgent repair is indicated for a symptomatic, tender or ruptured aneurysm, and he has no pain and no tenderness with a stable growth rate. Operating at 4.8 cm exposes him to perioperative mortality that exceeds his current annual rupture risk. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Reassure him and repeat the ultrasound only if he develops abdominal symptoms
options.rationale: Symptom triggered imaging fails because the first symptom of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is frequently rupture, which carries a mortality of around eighty percent when all prehospital deaths are counted. Surveillance exists precisely because the condition is silent until it is catastrophic. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Arrange interval ultrasound surveillance with cardiovascular risk factor treatment
options.rationale: Repair is offered at 5.5 cm in men, for growth exceeding 1 cm in a year, or for symptoms, and at 4.8 cm growing 0.2 cm over eleven months he meets none of these, so surveillance at intervals of around six months is correct. The active part of management is cardiovascular, since smoking cessation is the single most effective measure for slowing expansion and statin and antihypertensive treatment address the coronary disease that is the commonest cause of death in these patients. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Start a beta blocker specifically to slow the rate of aneurysm expansion
options.rationale: Beta blockade was studied for this purpose on the rationale of reducing aortic wall stress and randomised trials showed no reduction in expansion rate or rupture. It remains appropriate if indicated for another reason such as ischaemic heart disease, which he does not have. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Order computed tomography angiography now to plan endovascular stent grafting
options.rationale: Computed tomography angiography is the planning study once the repair threshold is reached, as it defines neck anatomy and iliac access for stent grafting. Performing it eight months before he is likely to need it adds contrast and radiation exposure without changing anything today. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

explanation.summary: Elective repair of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm is offered at a maximum diameter of 5.5 cm in men, at around 5.0 cm in women, for expansion exceeding 1 cm per year, or for symptoms or tenderness regardless of size. Below those thresholds the annual rupture risk is lower than the perioperative mortality of repair, so surveillance is the correct approach, with ultrasound intervals shortening as the diameter increases. This man is at 4.8 cm with 0.2 cm of growth over eleven months, which is well within the surveillance range. The most effective intervention available to him is smoking cessation, which slows expansion and reduces rupture risk, and he has already achieved it. Optimising blood pressure and lipids matters because most patients with an aneurysm die of coronary disease rather than of rupture.
key_points: Repair thresholds are 5.5 cm in men, around 5.0 cm in women, growth over 1 cm per year, or symptoms.
Below the threshold the perioperative mortality of repair exceeds the annual rupture risk.
Smoking cessation is the single most effective measure for slowing aneurysm expansion.
Beta blockers have been trialled for expansion and do not slow it.
Most patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm die of coronary disease rather than of rupture.
explanation.pearls: Treat an incidentally found aneurysm below 5.5 cm as a cardiovascular diagnosis rather than a surgical one, because the patient is statistically far likelier to die of coronary disease than of rupture, and smoking cessation does more to slow expansion than any drug that has been trialled.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

subtopic_detail: investigating persistent symptoms twelve months after starting a gluten free diet for coeliac disease
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman diagnosed with coeliac disease twelve months ago on duodenal biopsy showing subtotal villous atrophy. She started a gluten free diet immediately after diagnosis.

She reports that her bloating and loose stools improved for about four months and have since returned, occurring most days. She has not lost weight, has no nocturnal diarrhoea, no rectal bleeding and no fever. She eats out two or three times a week and buys packaged foods, and she has not seen a dietitian since the month after her diagnosis. Her tissue transglutaminase antibody was 128 units at diagnosis, fell to 34 at six months and is 41 units today. Her haemoglobin and ferritin have normalised on oral iron and her albumin is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with mild distension, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, no dermatitis herpetiformis, body mass index 24 kg/m2 and unchanged from diagnosis
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase antibody 128 units at diagnosis, 34 at six months and 41 today, haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-300), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist dietitian to review adherence and hidden exposure
options.rationale: Continuing gluten exposure, usually inadvertent, accounts for the great majority of persistent symptoms after diagnosis, and a serology that has plateaued and then risen rather than normalising is the objective marker of ongoing exposure. Cross contamination in restaurant kitchens, shared toasters and gluten in sauces, medications and supplements are not identifiable without a specialist dietary history, which is why this precedes any further investigation. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Start oral budesonide for presumed refractory coeliac disease and reassess
options.rationale: Refractory coeliac disease is treated with corticosteroid and is diagnosed only after persistent villous atrophy is demonstrated on repeat biopsy with strict adherence confirmed, which has not been established here. It is also rare, affecting a very small proportion of patients, and her rising serology points to exposure rather than to true refractoriness. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Arrange computed tomography enterography to exclude small bowel lymphoma
options.rationale: Enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma is a recognised complication and is sought when there are alarm features such as weight loss, fever, night sweats, abdominal pain or a falling albumin. She has none of these and her weight, albumin and inflammatory markers are all normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Trial a low fermentable carbohydrate diet for coexisting irritable bowel syndrome
options.rationale: Functional gut symptoms genuinely coexist with coeliac disease and a low fermentable carbohydrate approach helps those patients, and it is considered only once ongoing gluten exposure has been excluded. Layering a second restrictive diet onto an incompletely implemented first one makes both harder to follow. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Repeat duodenal biopsy now to assess whether the villous architecture has recovered
options.rationale: Repeat biopsy has a place in assessing mucosal healing and is essential before diagnosing refractory disease, and performed while adherence is unverified it cannot distinguish ongoing exposure from true refractoriness. The dietary assessment should come first so the biopsy, if still needed, can be interpreted. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

explanation.summary: Persistent or recurrent symptoms after a coeliac diagnosis are common, and continuing gluten exposure accounts for the large majority of cases. Serology is the most useful objective guide: antibody titres should fall progressively and normalise within about twelve months of strict adherence, so a plateau or a rise indicates ongoing exposure even when the patient believes the diet is strict. Common sources are cross contamination in shared kitchens and restaurants, and gluten in sauces, thickeners, medications and supplements, none of which emerge without a detailed dietary review. Refractory coeliac disease and enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma are important but rare, and both are pursued only after adherence has been verified or when alarm features are present. Coexisting functional gut symptoms are considered once exposure has been excluded.
key_points: Ongoing gluten exposure explains most persistent symptoms after a coeliac diagnosis.
Antibody titres should fall progressively and normalise within about twelve months of strict adherence.
A plateau or rise in serology is objective evidence of continuing exposure.
Refractory coeliac disease requires demonstrated persistent villous atrophy with verified adherence.
Weight loss, fever, night sweats, pain or falling albumin are alarm features prompting imaging for lymphoma.
explanation.pearls: Plot the coeliac serology trend rather than reading a single value, because a titre that falls and then plateaus or rises is objective evidence of continuing gluten exposure and sends the patient to a dietitian rather than to repeat endoscopy.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

subtopic_detail: lowering an extreme triglyceride concentration after an episode of pancreatitis with lipaemic serum
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38 year old man on day four of an admission with acute pancreatitis. His abdominal pain has settled and he has resumed a light oral diet.

The laboratory reported his admission serum as grossly lipaemic. His abdominal ultrasound showed no gallstones and no biliary dilatation, and his admission alcohol history is twelve standard drinks most evenings for several years. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone and has not attended review for two years. His admission triglycerides were 46 mmol/L and are 18 mmol/L today after fasting and insulin infusion. His amylase peaked at four times the upper limit of normal. He has eruptive xanthomas over both elbows and his father had pancreatitis in his forties.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Crops of yellow papules over both elbows and knees, no tendon xanthomas, no corneal arcus, abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, body mass index 33 kg/m2, hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Triglycerides 46 mmol/L on admission and 18 mmol/L today (less than 2.0), total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L (less than 5.5), haemoglobin A1c 82 mmol/mol (less than 53), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 45), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, lipase raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to prevent a further episode?

options.text: Fenofibrate with alcohol abstinence, dietary fat restriction and glycaemic control
options.rationale: Fibrates activate peroxisome proliferator activated receptor alpha and are the most effective agents for lowering triglycerides, reducing them by up to half, which is what is needed to move him below the threshold at which pancreatitis recurs. The drug alone is insufficient because alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes and dietary fat are each driving the hypertriglyceridaemia, so treating all four factors together is what prevents another episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: High intensity statin therapy titrated to a target low density lipoprotein level
options.rationale: Statins are the cornerstone of cardiovascular risk reduction and lower triglycerides only modestly, typically by ten to thirty percent, which is insufficient at this concentration. He will need one for cardiovascular protection, but it does not address the pancreatitis risk that is the immediate problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Ezetimibe added to dietary modification with lipid review in three months
options.rationale: Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption and lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol with minimal effect on triglycerides. It addresses the wrong lipid fraction for a man whose risk comes from chylomicronaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Regular therapeutic plasma exchange arranged as an ongoing outpatient programme
options.rationale: Apheresis removes triglycerides rapidly and has a role in severe acute hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, particularly with organ failure, and in refractory familial chylomicronaemia. As ongoing outpatient therapy it is invasive and resource intensive when modifiable drivers have not yet been addressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Cholecystectomy on this admission to remove the likely source of the pancreatitis
options.rationale: Gallstones are the commonest cause of pancreatitis in Australia and cholecystectomy would be correct if they were present, and his ultrasound shows no stones and no biliary dilatation. Operating would not address the triglyceride concentration that caused this episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

explanation.summary: Hypertriglyceridaemia is the third commonest cause of acute pancreatitis after gallstones and alcohol, and the risk becomes appreciable above about 10 mmol/L and substantial above 20 mmol/L, when chylomicrons obstruct pancreatic capillaries and liberated free fatty acids injure acinar cells. Grossly lipaemic serum, eruptive xanthomas and a family history point to an underlying genetic predisposition unmasked by acquired factors, which here are alcohol, poorly controlled diabetes and obesity. Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride lowering drugs and are first line for preventing recurrence, with omega 3 fatty acids as a possible adjunct. Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and are prescribed for cardiovascular risk rather than for pancreatitis prevention. Controlling the acquired drivers is as important as the drug, because the genetic component alone rarely produces these concentrations.
key_points: Pancreatitis risk rises above about 10 mmol/L and becomes substantial above 20 mmol/L.
Eruptive xanthomas and lipaemic serum indicate chylomicronaemia.
Fibrates lower triglycerides by up to half and are first line for preventing recurrence.
Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and address cardiovascular rather than pancreatitis risk.
Alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes, obesity and certain drugs are the acquired drivers that must be corrected.
explanation.pearls: Treat the alcohol and the diabetes with the same urgency as the fibrate after hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, because a genetic predisposition rarely produces a triglyceride concentration above 20 mmol/L without an acquired driver, and the drug alone will not keep him below the threshold for recurrence.

subtopic_detail: separating drug induced prolactin elevation from a lactotroph adenoma when the level sits in an ambiguous range
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28 year old woman whose periods stopped seven months ago. She has a negative pregnancy test and has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples.

She was started on risperidone 3 mg daily fourteen months ago for a psychotic illness and has been stable on it since, with no relapse and good adherence. She takes no other medication, no herbal preparations and no opioids. She has no headache and no visual symptoms. Her thyroid function is normal, her renal function is normal and she has no features of polycystic ovary syndrome. Her prolactin measured on two occasions without venepuncture stress is 2 400 mIU/L and then 2 550 mIU/L. Her formal visual field testing is normal and her body mass index is 23 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible galactorrhoea, no goitre, no hirsutism or acne, visual fields full on formal perimetry, no cranial nerve abnormality, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2 400 mIU/L and 2 550 mIU/L on two occasions (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45-90), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, oestradiol low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange pituitary magnetic resonance imaging and liaise with her psychiatrist
options.rationale: Antipsychotic induced elevation usually sits below about 2 000 mIU/L, so a level above that range does not safely exclude a coexisting adenoma and imaging is required before the elevation is attributed to the drug. The psychiatrist must be involved because the alternatives, switching to a prolactin sparing agent such as aripiprazole or adding a dopamine agonist, both carry a risk of destabilising a psychotic illness that has been well controlled for over a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Stop the risperidone today and recheck the prolactin level in four weeks
options.rationale: Withdrawing the antipsychotic does test the hypothesis, and stopping it unilaterally in a woman whose psychotic illness has been stable for fourteen months risks relapse with far greater consequences than amenorrhoea. Any change to her antipsychotic belongs to a shared decision with the prescriber. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Start cabergoline to restore her menstrual cycle and continue the risperidone
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists lower prolactin effectively and are first line for a true lactotroph adenoma, and in a patient on an antipsychotic they directly oppose the dopamine blockade that is treating her illness and can precipitate psychotic relapse. They are used in this setting only with psychiatric agreement and after imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Reassure her that this is an expected drug effect and no further action is needed
options.rationale: Attributing it to the drug without imaging accepts a diagnosis that the level does not support, and it also leaves prolonged hypo-oestrogenism untreated, which causes accelerated bone loss in a woman of 28. An expected adverse effect still requires management when it is causing harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Request macroprolactin screening on the stored sample before doing anything further
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive complex that causes a spuriously high result and is worth excluding in an asymptomatic patient with an unexplained elevation. She has galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and a low oestradiol, which demonstrate that the circulating prolactin is biologically active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics that block the dopamine D2 receptor remove the tonic inhibition of lactotrophs by hypothalamic dopamine and raise prolactin, with risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride the worst offenders while aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are comparatively sparing. The difficulty is that drug induced elevation and a prolactinoma present identically with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, so the magnitude of the elevation is used as a guide. Drug induced levels usually remain below about 2 000 mIU/L, and levels above that range warrant pituitary imaging before the elevation is attributed to medication. Prolonged hypo-oestrogenism carries real consequences for bone density, so the problem cannot simply be accepted. Management requires collaboration with the psychiatrist, since both switching the antipsychotic and adding a dopamine agonist risk destabilising the underlying illness.
key_points: Dopamine D2 blockade removes tonic inhibition of lactotrophs and raises prolactin.
Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin most, while aripiprazole and quetiapine spare it.
Drug induced elevation usually stays below about 2 000 mIU/L, and higher levels warrant pituitary imaging.
Macroprolactin causes spuriously raised results but does not cause galactorrhoea or amenorrhoea.
Prolonged hypo-oestrogenism from hyperprolactinaemia accelerates bone loss and must be addressed.
explanation.pearls: Image the pituitary rather than blaming the antipsychotic when prolactin exceeds about 2 000 mIU/L, and never stop or add to a psychotropic regimen unilaterally, because both switching the agent and starting a dopamine agonist can precipitate relapse of a psychotic illness that has been stable for a year.
